title: Clinician personal safety and workplace violence
summary: Health and social care workers face more workplace violence than most workers, and clinicians can also be stalked or harassed online. Employers and practices share responsibility for prevention: room set-up, alarms, check-in rules for home and community visits, training in de-escalation, and support after an incident. Codes allow clinicians to end services when they are threatened, with referral when possible. This page is information, not legal advice.
keyPoints: US federal workplace safety guidance for health care and social service workers describes five parts of a prevention program: leadership commitment and worker involvement, worksite analysis, hazard prevention and control, training, and recordkeeping with program review.
Office: keep a clear path to the door for both people, remove objects that could be used as weapons, have a way to call for help, and avoid being alone in the building for higher-risk sessions.
Home and community visits: share your itinerary, check in and out with a named person, keep your phone charged, park for an easy exit, and leave if a situation feels unsafe.
Online: limit personal information on public profiles, use separate work accounts, and know your options, such as address confidentiality programs and protective orders, if you are stalked.
After an incident: get medical care if needed, report it, talk it through with a supervisor or peer, and decide with support whether treatment can safely continue or should be transferred.
Codes allow ending therapy when you are threatened or endangered by the client or someone close to them (for example APA Standard 10.10).
A threat against someone else may trigger duties to warn or protect; see that topic.
whatToDo: Review your office and visit procedures with your team, including alarms, exits and check-in rules.
Train in de-escalation and agree a code word or signal for calling help.
Record threats and incidents, and follow your organization's reporting process.
Plan how to end or transfer care safely when a client has threatened you, and document the reasons.
Consult your employer's safety lead, your licensing board or a healthcare attorney about reporting, protective orders and ending services.
questions: If this session went badly, how would I get out and get help?
Does someone know where I am and when to expect me back?
What personal information about me can a client find online?
After a threat, can I keep working with this client safely and effectively?
